findings.title: Password change no longer rotates session_secret, so stolen or other-device session cookies stay valid (session-hijack persistence)
findings.problem: The diff removes the session_secret rotation from change_password. new_auth now updates only password_hash (line 1567). Session cookies are checked by validate_session(cookie, auth.session_secret) in middleware.py:146 and routes.py:1357, and the cookie is signed over the username with session_secret only. It never binds to password_hash. So after a password change, every cookie issued earlier still validates for the full COOKIE_MAX_AGE window (30 days, auth.py:10). middleware.py:197-206 also re-signs sessions on the sliding refresh, so an attacker's stolen cookie can be extended indefinitely. No same-purpose replacement found. The only remaining rotation is the reset flow at routes.py:1941-1945. The removed comment states the intended behavior: when a user changes their password because a session may be compromised, all other devices are logged out. That guarantee is now gone.
findings.fix_hint: restore generate_session_secret() rotation in new_auth and re-issue the acting user's cookie under the new secret (mirror the reset_password path at routes.py:1941-2009)
findings.why_it_matters: A user who changes their password after a suspected compromise is not protected. The attacker's session keeps working, and middleware refresh can keep it alive with no limit.
source_window: context={"errors": {"new_password": "Password must be 72 characters or fewer"}},

members.title: change_password no longer rotates session_secret, leaving stolen/compromised sessions valid after a password change
members.problem: The diff deletes the session_secret rotation, the re-issued cookie for the acting session, and the confirmation log line from the authenticated change_password handler. Because session_secret is unchanged, every pre-existing cookie continues to validate after the password is changed. This is a clean revert of a prior, deliberate fix: .planning/milestones/v2.6-phases/58-auth-test-suite/58-SECURITY.md records that threat T-58-07 was originally accepted and was later explicitly REVOKED/superseded on 2026-05-31 when change_password was changed to rotate session_secret, specifically to mitigate CWE-613. .planning/STATE.md:78 documents the same fix (commits 0866332 + 0e745ab, deep-reviewed APPROVED). reset_confirm_post (routes.py:1937-2011) still rotates session_secret, reissues the cookie, and logs. Existing tests tests/test_auth_routes.py:604, :641, :677, and tests/test_auth_integration.py:182 all assert the exact behavior this diff removes and will now fail.
source_window: context={"errors": {"new_password": "Password must be 72 characters or fewer"}},
members.why_it_matters: If an attacker has stolen a session cookie, the standard remediation users rely on, changing the password to kick out anyone else, silently does nothing: the attacker's cookie remains valid because session_secret never changes. This defeats the documented purpose of the control (CWE-613) and reopens a threat (T-58-07) the project had explicitly closed.
members.fix_hint: restore session_secret rotation on password change: generate a new session_secret, include it in the model_copy update alongside password_hash, persist it, and re-issue the acting user's cookie signed with the new secret (mirror the still-intact pattern in reset_confirm_post at routes.py:1937-2011)

members.title: change_password drops session-secret rotation, so it no longer matches reset_confirm_post and reverts a recorded v2.8.1 decision
members.problem: The codebase has one established way to change a credential: rotate session_secret with generate_session_secret(), persist it, then re-issue the acting user's cookie with sign_session(new_secret). Two places used it: change_password (before this diff) and reset_confirm_post (routes.py:1941-2010). The diff removes the pattern from change_password only, so reset_confirm_post is now the only credential-change path that rotates. The intent doc records rotation in change_password as a deliberate, reviewed fix that moved threat decision T-58-07 from accept to mitigate. Nothing in .planning authorizes undoing it.
source_window: context={"errors": {"new_password": "Password must be 72 characters or fewer"}},
members.why_it_matters: Changing a password no longer logs out other devices, which brings back the CWE-613 exposure the project had already closed. The two credential-change paths now behave differently with no documented reason.
members.fix_hint: restore the generate_session_secret() rotation and the sign_session cookie re-issue in change_password, matching reset_confirm_post; if the revert is intentional, record the decision in STATE.md and the threat model first

intent_doc_match.quote: **Fix:** `change_password` now rotates `session_secret`, invalidating all other sessions on password change while re-issuing the acting user's cookie (CWE-613). Supersedes v2.6 threat decision T-58-07/AR-58-02 (was *accept*, now *mitigate*). Deep-reviewed (APPROVED), docs + threat model reconciled.

members.title: Changing the password no longer logs out other sessions: a stolen session cookie keeps working until it expires
members.problem: The diff removes the session_secret rotation from change_password. Session cookies are just the username signed with session_secret (triggarr/auth.py:79-94, TimestampSigner), and validate_session (triggarr/auth.py:97-115) checks only that signature and max_age. Nothing ties a cookie to password_hash. So after this change, a password change leaves every existing cookie valid on every device, including one an attacker took. No replacement found: middleware.py:146 and routes.py:1357 both call validate_session with only auth.session_secret. The reset-token flow at routes.py:1941-2005 still rotates the secret, so the two password paths are now inconsistent.
source_window: context={"errors": {"new_password": "Password must be 72 characters or fewer"}},
members.why_it_matters: A user who changes their password because they think a session was compromised gets no protection. The attacker's cookie keeps admin access to the Triggarr UI and its API keys for the full COOKIE_MAX_AGE window.
members.fix_hint: Restore the generate_session_secret() rotation and re-issue the acting user's cookie, as the removed block did and as the reset flow at routes.py:1941-2005 still does.

members.title: Stolen session cookies retain access after password changes
members.problem: Updating only password_hash preserves the session signing secret. An attacker can replay a previously stolen triggarr_session cookie after the owner changes their password: AuthMiddleware (triggarr/web/middleware.py:144-148) accepts it using validate_session, which checks only the signature and 30-day expiry, never the password hash. Removing secret rotation therefore preserves attacker access for the cookie's remaining lifetime. Existing session-eviction tests explicitly require the opposite behavior.
source_window: context={"errors": {"new_password": "Password must be 72 characters or fewer"}},
members.why_it_matters: Updating only password_hash preserves the session signing secret. An attacker can replay a previously stolen triggarr_session cookie after the owner changes their password. Existing session-eviction tests explicitly require the opposite behavior.
members.fix_hint: Restore atomic password-hash and session-secret rotation, and reissue the acting user's cookie using the new secret. Preserve the existing session-eviction assertions.

findings.title: Four existing tests that check session rotation on password change will fail
findings.problem: tests/test_auth_routes.py:604 (test_change_password_rotates_session_secret_and_persists) and three sibling tests at :645, :681 and :713 assert rotation, a persisted new session_secret and a re-issued cookie. The handler no longer rotates the secret or sets a cookie, so those assertions should fail. That breaks the CLAUDE.md pre-push gate (pytest tests/ -x). The suite was not run.
findings.fix_hint: Restoring rotation fixes this. If dropping rotation is intentional, the tests must be rewritten, which would amount to accepting the security regression.
findings.why_it_matters: CI and the deep-review gate turn red. It also shows the removed behavior was an intended, tested part of the design (decision D-12 lineage).
